differences.title: 1. CONFIG MODEL
differences.leftDesc: NGINX uses a largely static, file-based configuration model (directives compiled into worker behavior). Reloads apply changes by spinning up new workers with updated config, typically minimizing downtime via graceful reload semantics.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy is designed for dynamic configuration via xDS (CDS/EDS/RDS/LDS). Proxies fetch route/clusters/listeners over a control plane and apply updates incrementally, enabling fleet-wide changes without full process reloads.

differences.title: 2. EXTENSIBILITY
differences.leftDesc: NGINX extends through built-in modules and third-party C modules, plus commercial variants. Extensions run in-process with NGINX event loops, so feature additions often trade flexibility for predictable performance and a tighter deployment model.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy’s extensibility is first-class: HTTP filters and network filters with stable interfaces. It also supports out-of-process extensions (e.g., via gRPC/HTTP), isolating custom logic and evolving capabilities without forking the proxy.

differences.title: 3. HTTP ROUTING & MATCHING
differences.leftDesc: NGINX routing is built around location blocks with precedence rules and can use regex locations. For high scale, correct ordering and regex choices matter because matching occurs per request within worker logic.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy uses structured route configuration with ordered route lists and matcher types (prefix, exact, headers, safe regex). Matching is designed to be deterministic and efficiently evaluated, then drives per-route policy (clusters, retries, timeouts).

differences.title: 4. LOAD BALANCING BEHAVIOR
differences.leftDesc: NGINX load balancing is configured per upstream and typically selects backends using algorithms like round-robin, least connections, or hash. Health checks and failover are configurable, but state is managed within each worker/upstream context.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy load balancing is cluster-centric: each cluster maintains per-endpoint state (health, metadata) and supports multiple LB policies (round_robin, least_request, ring_hash). Outlier detection can eject unhealthy hosts based on real-time observations.

differences.title: 5. STREAMING & TIMEOUT CONTROL
differences.leftDesc: NGINX exposes granular directives for connection lifetimes, read/write timeouts, buffering, and proxy buffering behavior. These knobs directly shape how the event loop handles slow clients and streaming responses at the socket level.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy models timeouts and retry budgets as explicit per-route and per-virtual-host policies (e.g., idle timeout, request timeout). It also separates connection-level vs request-level behavior, improving control for streaming and long-lived RPC-like HTTP.

differences.title: 6. OBSERVABILITY DEFAULTS
differences.leftDesc: NGINX observability commonly relies on access/error logs plus metric exports via add-ons. For deeper telemetry (routes, retries), teams often augment with modules or integrate external exporters.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy ships with structured stats and rich telemetry primitives (counters, gauges, histograms) and integrates cleanly with OpenTelemetry-style tracing. Route/cluster decisions, retries, and upstream health events can be reflected in emitted signals.

differences.title: 7. NETWORK PROTOCOL POSITIONING
differences.leftDesc: NGINX is a common edge reverse proxy and ingress controller, optimized for static, high-throughput deployments. It excels when you want predictable behavior with minimal moving parts and strong operational familiarity.
differences.rightDesc: Envoy is often adopted as the data-plane in service meshes and as an edge proxy for distributed systems. Its design centers on consistent L7 policy enforcement across many services with dynamic discovery and coordinated rollout.
